title: APE-Bench: Evaluating Automated Proof Engineering for Formal Math Libraries
claim: A benchmark and its evaluation harness decompose into a construction pipeline, richer task format than prior benchmarks, and modular infrastructure.
layout: 3 regions: top pipeline left-to-right, bottom comparison panels plus architecture block diagram
description: A muted beige and brown figure in monospace type, split into a top strip and a bottom area. The top strip is a left-to-right pipeline: repo commits (stacked file-tree cards), then human diff (bars marked with red minus and plus lines), then an instruction card, then an agent patch. The patch leads to a stacked Lean compile and LLM judge box. The bottom left has two small panels, miniF2F and miniCTX, each showing a theorem statement with navy proof bars below it. The bottom middle shows APE-Bench as a long code file with red highlighted edits, struck-through lines, and a red arrow labelled apply patch. The bottom right is the APE-Harness architecture. An orchestrator holds Task Data and Task Config. These feed a task runner that contains a toolkit (bash, file system, Lean compile, Lean retrieve, submit result), a scaffold (LLMs) and workspaces (scratch, target, reference). Task Criteria and Task Result sit at the bottom. The red code panel draws the eye first.
caption: APE framework overview. Top: Benchmark construction and evaluation pipeline. Bottom: Evaluation paradigm comparison (miniF2F/miniCTX, APE-Bench) and APE-Harness infrastructure architecture (task contracts, scaffolds, toolkits, workspaces).
abstract: While frontier formal mathematics systems now routinely develop repository-scale proof engineering artifacts requiring multi-file coordination and semantic correctness beyond compilation, existing evaluation benchmarks remain focused on isolated theorem proving. We introduce Automated Proof Engineering (APE), the first systematic framework for evaluating repository-scale proof engineering through dual verification that validates both syntactic compilation and semantic requirement satisfaction in pinned library environments. We present a complete infrastructure comprising APE-Bench, which automatically extracts proof engineering tasks from real library commit histories, and APE-Harness, a unified execution framework based on task contract abstraction. This contract-based design enables standardized evaluation across diverse formal mathematics tasks and fair systematic comparison of different agent implementations (including our APE-Agent reference scaffold alongside Claude Code and Codex CLI) on identical task specifications. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness through comprehensive evaluation. All code and benchmark dataset are released as open-source at https://github.com/xinhjBrant/APE-Bench.
